statement: Everest is an unincorporated community in Everest Township, Cass County, North Dakota, United States.
Everest is located south of Casselton.
Everest was platted in 1881.
The post office in Everest was established in 1882 and operated until 1908.
Everest was originally at the junction of the Great Northern Railway and the Northern Pacific Railway.
The westernmost of the two rail lines in Everest was removed circa 1896 when it was acquired by the Great Northern Railway.
Everest was the birthplace of North Dakota governor (and later US senator) William Langer.
The Langer family, including William's father Frank and uncle Joseph, were prominent residents of the Everest area during the late 1800s.
Noted residents of Everest included James Trammell, Edward Meilicke, Edward Redmon, Edward Weber, Edward Arnold, William MacFadden, and August Hilke.
Each of the noted residents (James Trammell, Edward Meilicke, Edward Redmon, Edward Weber, Edward Arnold, William MacFadden, and August Hilke) served as Everest Township or Cass County officials.
Other prominent residents of Everest included Herbert Nilles, who was elected to the presidency of the North Dakota State Bar.
Morgan Ford, another prominent resident, was appointed as a judge to the US Customs Court.

Everest was the site of a railroad depot, a post office, two hotels, a school, a church, two general stores, two saloons, a butcher shop, a blacksmith shop, a lumber yard, four grain elevators, a harness maker, and other businesses.
Everest once reported over 200 residents and was considered a prosperous community in the late 1800s.
The removal of the rail line, closure of the post office, and a series of disastrous fires led to a decline in the Everest community.
By 1960, most of Everest's establishments had long since closed.
Everest had a population of 10 in 1960.
Everest has been removed from official county maps.
Everest is 20 miles (32 km) from Fargo, which is the county seat.
Everest is 2 miles (3.2 km) south of Casselton.
Everest lies at the junction of North Dakota Highway 18 and 155th Avenue SE, near the Casselton Robert Miller Regional Airport.
Everest is mostly located in section 15 of Everest Township, in southeastern North Dakota.
The Durbin-Everest Channel, an intermittent stream, flows south of Everest.
The Wheatland Channel, another intermittent stream, runs north of Everest.
Both the Durbin-Everest Channel and the Wheatland Channel are tributaries of Swan Creek.
Everest began as a railroad station on the St. Paul, Minneapolis, and Manitoba Railway, also known as the Great Northern Railway.
In August 1880, the Casselton Branch Railroad Company (CB) was incorporated by the Northern Pacific Railway (NP).
Construction began on a railroad line joining the Northern Pacific's railroad in Cass County with a station in Traill County.
Everest was platted in 1881, with the town divided into twelve blocks.
The east–west streets in Everest were named A, B, C, and D Streets.
The north–south streets in Everest were named Front, Second, Third, and Fourth Streets.
Manvell Street ran diagonally along the line of the Great Northern Railroad.
The community of Everest was built directly west and south of the rail line.
By the late 1880s, Everest was considered a 'small town in Cass County [...] some 20 miles from Fargo.'
There is some controversy surrounding the naming of the Everest community.
Some sources report that the community was named after Charles Everitt, the editor of The Lisbon Star.
During the summer of 1881, Everest was in development.
The railroad line between Casselton and Everest had not yet been completed in the summer of 1881.
A stagecoach line connected Casselton and Everest in the summer of 1881.
The first hotel in Everest was a primitive affair.
Mary E. Hogue Black, a schoolteacher in Casselton, reported on her experience traveling to Everest by stagecoach due to an uncompleted railroad line between Casselton and Everest.
In October 1882, an agreement between the Northern Pacific and the Great Northern railroads transferred the Casselton Branch from the Northern Pacific to the Great Northern Railway.
The Great Northern then began a project to connect the 3 miles (4.8 km) between its lines to the Casselton Branch terminus at Everest.
The rail line connecting the two railroads was announced to be nearing completion in October 1882.
After completion of the connection, Everest was at the junction of the Waupeton-Ripon railroad line (between Durbin and Sidney) and the Casselton-Larimore rail line (at the terminus of that line).
The Everest post office was established on May 24, 1882.
Carl Knoppel was the postmaster of Everest.
On January 18, 1884, Everest Township was established.
Everest Township, along with Walberg Township, were the first civil townships established in Cass County.
By 1884, Everest was the site of two general stores, a butcher shop, a blacksmith shop, a lumber yard, and two hotels.
One of the hotels in Everest in 1884 proudly advertised its fine horses.
In 1884, Everest had a post office and a one-room school.
The postmaster in 1884 was J.H. Rodenberg.
William Langer, who later twice served as governor of North Dakota, was born in Everest in 1886.
William Langer served as governor from 1933 to 1934, and from 1937 to 1939.
William Langer's father, Frank, co-owned Everest's first general store.
Frank Langer had also helped establish the community of Everest, as he was an investor in new towns.
Frank Langer became the postmaster in 1884.
In 1889, Frank Langer was elected to the 11th district in the lower house of the newly created North Dakota state legislature.
Frank Langer served one term in the state legislature and then returned to farming.
Frank Langer later became a Cass County commissioner.
The Langer family later moved to nearby Casselton.
William Langer graduated from Casselton High School.
Frank's brother Joseph Langer was born on January 22, 1852.
Joseph Langer moved to Dakota Territory with Frank and helped establish the community of Everest.
Joseph Langer claimed a tree farm in Everest Township in 1877.
Joseph Langer also invested in a mercantile in Hope.
Joseph Langer was a member of the Masonic Lodge.
Joseph Langer served on the Everest Township board of supervisors for over a decade.
The Langer family eventually owned many parcels of land surrounding Everest, Casselton, and other neighboring townships.

Olsen (1967) reported that the Langer family owned eleven quarters in Everest Township, three quarters in Maple River Township, two quarters in Casselton Township, and much of the south half of section 35 in Casselton Township.
An atlas showed that Joseph Langer owned fourteen quarters of land in Casselton and Everest townships in 1906.
Edward Meilicke farmed in Everest Township and operated a mercantile in the community.
Meilicke settled in the Everest area in 1882.
Edward Meilicke served for 15 years as the chairman of the Everest Township board of supervisors.
Edward Meilicke was later profiled in an early history of North Dakota.
August Hilke was born in Germany on November 18, 1837.
August Hilke was among the earliest of the white settlers in Cass County.
Hilke's family emigrated to Dodge County, Wisconsin in the United States in 1852.
Hilke moved to Casselton in 1878.
Hilke settled in section 23 of Everest Township in 1880.
Hilke's wife passed in 1884.
Hilke married Cora Clark in 1885.
August Hilke became a member of the Cass County board of supervisors.
August Hilke was the school treasurer.
August Hilke joined the Odd Fellows and the Ancient Order of United Workmen.

In 1900, according to one state history, August Hilke was 'the fortunate possessor of one of the best farms of Cass County, and his residence on section 23, of Everest Township, is evidence of his prosperity and thrift.'
James D. Trammell was a prominent resident of Everest.
Trammell was a transplant from Fairfax County, Virginia.
James D. Trammell settled in Everest in 1883.
Trammell served on the Everest Township board of supervisors.
Trammell was a member of the area's Masonic Hall and Odd Fellows fraternal order.
Edward Redmon was born in Davenport, Iowa in 1856.
Edward Redmon moved to the Everest area in 1877 to claim land.
Edward Redmon owned three sections of land and also farmed in a fourth.
Edward Redmon was a chairman of the Everest Township board of supervisors for many years.
William MacFadden was born in Mount Vernon, Ohio in 1857.
William MacFadden emigrated to Everest in 1885.
William MacFadden became a grain buyer and farmer in Everest, purchasing land there.
William MacFadden was appointed deputy county treasurer.
William MacFadden later became the cashier of the Cass County State Bank of Casselton.
William MacFadden was elected as Cass County treasurer in 1894 and was re-elected in 1896.
Edward Weber was born in Landskron, Austria, on September 28, 1849.
Edward Weber came to the United States in 1867.
Edward Weber married Rosa Stanger in 1871.
Edward Weber visited Cass County in 1877 with Frank and Joseph Langer.
Edward Weber settled in section 9 of Everest Township, where he bought land for himself, his brother, and his father circa 1877.
By 1900, Edward Weber owned five sections of land in the Everest area.
Edward Weber served as an Everest Township official and also worked as a county assessor.
Circa 1888, Everest was the site of four grain elevators: the Cargill Elevator Company, the St. Anthony Elevator Company, the Northwestern Elevator Company, and the Mt. Vernon Elevator Company.
Everest was also the site of a branch of the Beidler and Robinson Lumber Company.
The population of Everest was estimated as 200 in 1890.
The Everest School was built in 1881.
The Everest School was originally located in a field 0.5 miles (0.80 km) west of the main structures.
A rope was strung between the village and the school to prevent schoolchildren from becoming lost during snowstorms.
The Everest School was eventually moved into the village.
The Everest School District was originally numbered 102.
The Everest school building, a one-room schoolhouse, was one of 182 schools in Cass County at that time.
Two teachers were employed by the Everest school during that era.
The Everest school building was also used as an official polling location.
Two additional schools operated in the Everest area: the Goshen School and the Langer School.
The Goshen School and the Langer School were small Everest Township schools.
In November 1886, a fire destroyed part of Everest, including the business district.
The 1886 fire made state headlines.
The 1886 fire destroyed Rodenberg and Langer's general store, two saloons, the hotel, McFadden and Siddell's hardware store, Wilson's boarding house, and the post office.
The 1886 fire began in a vacant hotel room.
The Moravian Church operated in Everest circa 1887.
William Stengel led the Moravian congregation in Everest circa 1887.
In 1888, severe frosts in May, June, and August affected the wheat crop in the Red River Valley.
The eastern half of the state was badly affected by the 1888 frosts.
The following year (1889), there was a terrible drought in Dakota, which destroyed the next round of crops.
Area farmers suffered, and many were close to starvation due to the frosts and drought.
Frank Langer, one of the county commissioners, advocated for a poor farm to be located in nearby Casselton.
Frank Langer was outvoted by the other Cass County commissioners regarding the poor farm location.
The poor farm was built 3.5 miles (5.6 km) north of Fargo.
Everest had been founded in Cass County, in the northern half of Dakota Territory.
North Dakota and South Dakota were split and became states on November 2, 1889.
When the new state of North Dakota's first territorial legislature met, the state was divided into 31 congressional districts.

The 11th Congressional District was a portion of Cass County, including the townships of Webster, Rush River, Hunter, Arthur, Amenia, Everest, Maple River, Leonard, Dows, Erie, Empire, Wheatland, Gill, Walburg, Watson, Page, Rich, Ayr, Buffalo, Howes, Eldrid, Highland, Rochester, Lake, Cornell, Tower, Hill, Clifton and Pontiac.
The 11th Congressional District was entitled to one state senator and three state representatives.
Everest resident Frank J Langer was among the state representatives for the 11th Congressional District.
In March 1894, the business district of Everest was again wiped out by fire.
The 1894 fire was estimated to have done $35,000 in damage (equivalent to $1,132,000 in 2024).

At the time of the 1894 fire, the Hope (North Dakota) Pioneer reported that 'The town of Everest, Cass county, was nearly wiped out of existence by fire early Sunday morning. Jim Hill's depot didn't burn, much to the regret of all the travelers along the line who have been compelled to wait upon trains within its dirty walls.'
Around 1895 or 1896, the westernmost of the two railroad lines was pulled up because the Great Northern Railroad Company's plans for expansion had changed.
The removed rail line was 4.79 miles (7.71 km)-long and connected the towns of Everest and Fleming.
The removal was done because the Great Northern Railway was operating two parallel branch rail lines.
It was stated that 'for the sake of greater efficiency and the economy attained through elimination of unneeded trackage', the line between Fleming and Everest was no longer needed.
The removal of the rail line would, in retrospect, cause a decline for Everest.
In 1895, Everest was still considered a prosperous community.
An author writing in 1895 described 'The thriving towns of Everest, Casselton, and Amenia' and noted grain elevators towering above the flat lands, characteristic of the Red River Valley.
In 1900, a loading station on the Northern Pacific Railway was named Langers, after Joseph and Frank Langer.
The Langers station was just northeast of Everest.
The population of Everest was 213 in 1900.
Circa 1906, Everest was the site of three grain elevators: those of the St. Anthony and Dakota Elevator Company, the Cargill Elevator Company, and the Northwestern Elevator Company.
Everest received mail daily circa 1906.
Everest had telephone service circa 1906.
Everest was the site of a harness maker and a blacksmith shop circa 1906.
Stagecoaches ran daily between Everest and Casselton circa 1906.
The railroad depot in Everest closed in July 1903.
In 1903, there were reports that the Everest post office would close.
In 1903, Henry Albright succeeded James B. Coyle as the Everest postmaster.
Paul Schiebold was the postmaster circa 1906.
The Everest post office closed in 1908.
Mail for Everest was subsequently routed through nearby Casselton.
By the early twentieth century, several members of the Langer family had left Everest.
A new generation of businessmen operated in the Everest community in the early twentieth century.
Edward Arnold was born in Lockport, New York on March 18, 1874.
Edward Arnold relocated to Everest and was involved in the grain business by around 1914.
Edward Arnold became the manager of the Northwestern Elevator Company in Everest.
Edward Arnold became a well-known resident of the Everest community.
Edward Arnold was a member of the Ancient Order of United Workmen (AOUW) and the Brotherhood of American Yeomen (BAY).
Herbert G Nilles was born in Everest in 1894.
While in law school, Herbert G Nilles was a member of the Phi Delta Phi legal fraternity.
Herbert G Nilles was admitted to the North Dakota Bar in 1917.
In 1932, Herbert G Nilles was elected to membership in the North Dakota Chapter of the Order of the Coif.
Herbert G Nilles relocated to Fargo.
Herbert G Nilles was elected president of the State Bar Association of North Dakota in 1939.
Morgan Ford was born on a farm near Wheatland on September 8, 1911.
Morgan Ford was the son of Morgan J Ford and Mary Langer Ford.
After graduating from Casselton High School and the University of North Dakota, Morgan Ford returned to Cass County.
Morgan Ford taught at the Everest School for one year (1934-1935).
Morgan Ford became the Casselton city attorney in 1942.
Morgan Ford was nominated by President Harry S. Truman to be a judge of the United States Customs Court in 1949.
In 1920, the population of Everest was 64.
In 1922, there was again a fire in Everest.
The 1922 fire destroyed the Northwestern Elevator Company's building in Everest.

According to a news report in the Jamestown Weekly Alert, if the breeze had prevailed toward the stores southeast of the elevator, little would have been left of the town, and only hard work saved the depot.
According to the Jamestown Weekly Alert report, around 6,000 bushels of wheat were in the elevator at the time of the 1922 fire.
The cause of the 1922 fire was unknown.
One theory for the cause of the 1922 fire was sparks from the nearby railroad, or due to friction.
In 1923, the Everest School District covered 13.5 square miles (35 km2).
In 1923, Cass County had 142 operating schools.
The Everest School District had been renumbered 90 by 1923.
In 1928, a basement was added below the Everest Schoolhouse.
In 1939, the Langer School closed due to low enrollment.
During William Langer's gubernatorial race of 1936, it was reported that 100% of the residents of Everest Township voted for him.
It was claimed that all 63 voters of Everest Township endorsed William Langer during his Senate race of 1952.
The population of Everest was estimated at 100 in 1940.
The other communities along the former rail line were smaller in 1940, with Durbin reporting 22 residents and Fleming reporting 10 residents.
During the 1940s era, Everest still appeared on North Dakota state maps.
The general store in Everest closed in 1942.
In September 1949, enrollment at the Everest School was 17 students.
In 1952, William Langer, then a U.S. Senator, attempted to legally reclaim 2 acres (8,100 m2) of land in the Everest area.
The land William Langer attempted to reclaim had been deeded to the county in 1911 by his father, Frank Langer.
Langer stated that the contract stipulated that the land would be improved with a road and a bridge across a coulee.
Langer stated that no bridge or road had been constructed on the land.
Langer requested that the land be returned to the Langers.
William Langer passed away on November 8, 1959.
In 1960, Interstate 94 replaced State Highway 10 between Casselton and Everest, on the northern edge of Everest Township.
By 1960, the population of Everest had dropped to 10.
In 1962, the Everest School District #90 reported zero students.
In 1962, both the Everest School and the Goshen School closed.
The Everest School and the Goshen School were consolidated into the Casselton School District in 1962.
In 1968, the Casselton Elevator Company and feed plant burned to the ground.
The Casselton Elevator Company and feed plant was not rebuilt after the 1968 fire.
By 1975, Agnes Geelan wrote that Everest was just 'a memory, its chief claim to fame being that 'Bill Langer was born on a farm near Everest'.'
In 1979, it was reported that just four families lived in Everest.
No businesses remained in the Everest community in 1979.

Douglas Wick (1988) writes that 'the village existed for many years,' but its decline was aided by the closure of the railroad station and post office, the removal of one of the rail lines, and a disastrous fire.
Frank Weber, a longtime resident of Everest (beginning in 1893), blamed the automobile for the decline of Everest.
Frank Weber stated that 'Everest was a nice little town' and their 'home trading post' when they farmed on their home place.

Frank Weber stated that 'as soon as the automobile came the people then left Everest and went on to Casselton because there was more stores, and of course more selection of good and all this and that. And then all these little towns lost out, including Everest.'
Today, Everest is in the Central Cass Public School District.
Everest no longer appears on official county maps.
The population of all of Everest Township in 2020 was 36 residents, with 8 households.
